samples.hyp: Estimating the number of SARS-CoV-2 blanket tests required to potentially control the outbreak in Lusaka Province, Zambia, considering asymptomatic individuals:
Study of basic mathematics

The novel Coronavirus disease (COVID-19), caused by the severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2), in Africa has the highest number of asymptomatic (or mildly symptomatic) individuals who are thought to contribute to the spread of the disease.
The exact number and level of disease spread among asymptomatic individuals have not been clarified.
The study, however, indicated that managing them is crucial for controlling the spread of SARS-CoV-2.

We developed a simple, rapidly spreading susceptible-exposed-infectious-removed (SEIR) mathematical model to assess the impact of isolating asymptomatic but infectious SARS-CoV-2 cases through blanket testing to control the outbreak in Lusaka Province, Zambia.
Here we designed two scenarios; (1) asymptomatic individuals comprising 70% of all COVID-19 infections and (2) asymptomatic individuals comprising 50% of the population.

Meanwhile, the initial assessment of the sample was conducted under the assumption that asymptomatic individuals have the same transmission rate as symptomatic individuals, and secondly, and more likely, the assumption that asymptomatic individuals have half the transmission rate of symptomatic individuals.

For a model that captures asymptomatic cases at 70%, a lower daily testing rate of ≥ 7911 tests per 100,000 population is sufficient to control the outbreak if asymptomatic individuals are half as infectious, whereas if infection is assumed to be equal, a testing rate of ≥ 10028 tests per 100,000 population would be required.

For 50% of asymptomatic individuals, a low testing rate of ≥ 4540 tests per 100,000 population is sufficient to control the outbreak at all levels of disease transmission for asymptomatic individuals compared to symptomatic individuals.
Discussion and conclusion

Our model predicts that isolating COVID-19 cases, including asymptomatic ones, through blanket testing could be used as a potential measure to control the spread of SARS-CoV-2 in Lusaka, Zambia, but it will come at a cost.
Mass testing in major cities like Lusaka can limit the spread of COVID-19, but is it effective?
In the year 2020, computer models predicted that the spread of COVID-19 in major cities could be controlled through extensive testing and then isolating all those who were infected.
However, researchers say this method may be expensive and not useful.
At the beginning of the outbreak, many people who contracted COVID-19 did not show symptoms and still spread the virus to others.
Some studies have suggested that 50% to 80% of people with COVID-19 are asymptomatic and may be responsible for 40% to 70% of new infections.
Researchers wanted to know if identifying and isolating asymptomatic individuals would help in controlling the spread of COVID-19.
They also wanted to know if blanket testing, which means testing a large number of people indiscriminately, is effectively identifying asymptomatic individuals.
Researchers have developed a computer model that predicts how vulnerable individuals are to infection, as well as isolation.
They focused on data from the Lusaka province of Zambia, which is an integration hub with an international airport bordering two countries.

Due to the characteristics of COVID-19 appearing to vary from place to place, they considered 4 scenarios, where either 50% or 70% of those with COVID-19 were asymptomatic, and these cases were equally or half as likely to spread the virus as symptomatic individuals.
The researchers' model found that it is possible to control the spread of COVID-19 by conducting blanket testing and isolating all infected individuals, including those who are asymptomatic.
They said that to reduce the peak number of cases by 90% in all scenarios, 10% of the people in Lusaka need to be tested every day.
They also found that if we want to keep the number of new COVID-19 infections stable, 22% of people need to be tested every day.
Despite Zambia implementing numerous COVID-19 restriction measures, the infection rate is still rising.
Proper blanket testing should reduce the number of COVID-19 cases by 90% in a small town in Italy.
However, there is no previous research indicating that it would have an impact in a major city elsewhere.

Note that the researchers did not actually conduct a blanket test in this study; instead, they created a model that demonstrates how a blanket test would work to limit the spread of COVID-19 in major cities.
However, they warned that it would be very expensive.
They also said it could be more effective if combined with other measures, such as lockdowns, contact tracing, and vaccination.
Researchers in Zambia also emphasized that asymptomatic COVID-19 cases were more prevalent in Africa at that time.
Underrepresentation of genetic data in African populations due to genetic diversity and environmental factors.
The African population is underrepresented in genetic studies but has the greatest genetic diversity and faces various environmental advantages globally.

Because genetic prediction statistics have not yet been conducted in ancestors related to African diversity, we calculated polygenic risk scores (PRS) in simulations across Africa and expert data from South Africa and Uganda, as well as the UK, to further understand the study of genetic evolution.
The accuracy of PRS improves with study cohorts that match the ancestry compared to studies that do not match the ancestry.
Among the ancestors and ethnicities of South Africans, we found that the consistency of PRS is weak for each trait but varies among groups.
Differences among individuals of African descent contribute more to variations in PRS accuracy than other major group differences considered among people in the UK and Uganda.

We calculated PRS in African ancestral populations using large-scale European-only genome-wide association studies with diverse ancestral genetic studies; the enhanced variants resulted in the highest accuracy for aggregating haemoglobin and white blood cell count, indicating a significant effect of genetic ancestry in known loci influencing sickle cell disease and blood transfusion response, respectively.

Differences in the accuracy of PRS among individuals of African descent originating from different regions are as significant as those of non-African continental ancestors, requiring standardized values.
Why can't we accurately predict genetic diseases in people of African descent?
Researchers say that the current methods used to predict whether a person will contract a disease or not do not work well for people of African descent.
This is because the database that made such predictions mostly represents the genomes of people of European descent.
The GWAS database map refers to "Genome-Wide Association Studies", and scientists use it to search for traits and diseases related to genes.
In fact, they can use GWAS to estimate the genetic risk of a person for a disease or trait.
However, most of the genetic data in GWAS comes from individuals of European descent.
In this study, the researchers wanted to see how the calculations they use to determine the risk of genetic diseases using GWAS work for people of African descent.
Furthermore, they wanted to see if a diverse GWAS, meaning a database that includes more African genetic data, would improve predictions.
The calculation is known in scientific terms as "polygenic risk score", or PRS.

They used computers to calculate the risk predictions associated with the genetics of the African population using GWAS, and they utilized medical data of African individuals to examine certain traits or diseases caused by genetic variations.
When they used European GWAS, they found that the risk of genetic variants was more accurate if people had European ancestors compared to African natives for most traits.
They said the level of risk is not high among African regions because there are differences among communities, which does not align with what we see in European ancestors.
Researchers also stated that the accuracy of PRS increases as African ancestry decreases.
The Ethiopian population has gained a better understanding of genetic diseases since they have more similarities with the European population.
When using different GWAS that included people of African descent, the accuracy of predictions improved.
The prediction of blood diseases has been particularly accurate.
Previous studies have shown that PRS is limited for African populations, meaning that the GWAS databases have predicted a lower risk of genetic disorders for African people.
However, we know that this may not necessarily be true.

This study reveals that the low risk allele frequencies due to African genetic variants are underrepresented in the GWAS databases, therefore, the current PRS values do not significantly aid in predicting genetic diseases in Africa.
Researchers suggest that it would be better to use diverse data, including genetic information from African populations.
Therefore, further work is needed to enhance GWAS to include African ancestry so that we can accurately predict the risk of genetic diseases in African populations.
The authors of this study are from Africa, the USA, and the UK.
Evaluation of Visual and Genetic Testing in Preventing Cervical Dysplasia and Cervical Cancer in Namibia
An estimated 851,340 women in Namibia are at risk of contracting human papillomavirus (HPV), which can lead to cervical cancer.
The visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) and cryotherapy has been confirmed to be highly effective.
However, data related to the impact of cervical cancer screening programs is lacking.
This study evaluated visual inspection and cytology in the prevention of cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) and cervical cancer in Namibia.
Research indicates that women with HPV, cervicitis, koilocytosis, and atypia are at risk of testing positive for VIA.
Older women, especially those living with HIV, are more susceptible to developing skin cancers (SCC).
The VIA method appears to be useful in screening, although the screening procedure for patients in the Namibian context should be reviewed and used in conjunction with positive HR-HPV results.
Screening methods recommended include HPV testing at different ages and levels of risk (e.g., HIV-positive individuals, immunocompromised conditions).

The performance of assessment can be further enhanced by using a system that utilizes previous research results, women's health policies, modern education, and practices that are suitable for the geographical context.
Women in Namibia who are at risk of developing cervical cancer should be tested early and treated promptly.
Many tests can indicate the risk of women developing cervical cancer, but routine examinations in Namibia do not utilize these tests.
Researchers recommend regular testing to detect early warning signs, which could prevent women from contracting this rapidly fatal disease.
Cervical cancer (cancer of the cervix) causes the death of many women worldwide.
One of the factors that cause cervical cancer is the Human Papillomavirus, or HPV.
HPV is a virus that damages cervical cells, causing lesions, which can eventually become cancer.
Although there is a vaccine to prevent HPV infection, many women in African countries, including Namibia, do not have access to it.
This means that investigating the virus or the injuries it causes is particularly important for these women, as it is the most appropriate way to prevent cancer.
Researchers say that hospitals therefore need improved guidelines and information on the best tests to use.
They also added that healthcare workers need more information on how factors such as age or health affect a woman's risk of contracting HPV and cancer.
They investigated the impact of certain types of routine tests (known as screening methods) for detecting HPV infection and lesions.
They are also interested in comparing assessment methods, for example, collecting cervical cells for examining damage as opposed to only looking for lesions.
They also wanted to know whether differences among women, such as their age or if they have other diseases like HIV, altered their risk of contracting HPV and cancer.
Knowing this information can help hospitals and clinics to effectively utilize screening methods.
Researchers examined the patient records of 214 women who were tested for HPV infection, lesions, and cervical cancer at a hospital in Windhoek, Namibia.
They focused particularly on early-stage cervical cancer, which is when the disease can be treated easily and effectively.
They also collected data on the age of each woman, as well as her overall health.
By analyzing these data, they found that different screening technologies provide healthcare workers with different information, and they can be useful before or after HPV progresses to cancer.
For example, it is obtained by collecting and analyzing cervical cells.
Injuries can be detected, however, often only with visual inspection, using a technique called "visual inspection with acetic acid" (VIA).
The benefit of this technique is that it allows doctors to detect injuries quickly and inexpensively.
This is because it uses standard medical tools that have already been used for women's health examinations, such as a speculum (a metal instrument used to examine the inside of the vagina).
They also found that combining different methods often provides doctors with additional information about a woman's risk of developing cancer, especially through multiple screenings.
Moreover, researchers found that older women, especially those with HIV, are more susceptible to cancer, therefore, in many cases, testing them can be important.
The researchers added that few of the women were tested for HPV (before seeking lesions) despite the availability of the test.
Doing so can be an important way to detect the disease early.

Overall, they stated that their results indicate a need for a healthcare system in Namibia to design strategies for HPV and cervical cancer prevention with consideration, using affordable and effective testing methods to detect these diseases early.
The study was a collaboration between scientists from Namibia and South Africa.
The benefits of treatment in HBV/HIV co-infection compared to HBV alone in patients from South Africa

In launching the international goal to eliminate hepatitis B (HBV), we set out to compare individuals with HBV infection and those with dual infections, namely HBV/HIV, to assess the impact of treatment and guide improvements in clinical care.
We report observational data from a global real-world deep study cohort of 115 adults suffering from severe chronic hepatitis B (CHB), at a university hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
The presence of a virus and the HIV virus was found in 39 subjects (34%).
We documented detailed analytical data along with clinical and laboratory information.

Compared to those with another viral infection and HIV, adults with Hepatitis B infection are less likely to be HBeAg-positive (p=0.01), less likely to be assessed with elastography (p <0.0001), and less likely to be on antiviral therapy (p <0.0001); they were more likely to have Hepatitis B viraemia diagnosis (p=0.04), and more likely to have liver disease features including moderate/severe thrombocytopaenia (p=0.007), elevated bilirubin (p=0.004), and a high APRI score (p=0.02).
Three types of liver cancer all develop when there is HBV alone.

Our data indicate that individuals with HBV alone may be at a disadvantage compared to those with the HIV virus, suggesting a potential structural imbalance in the deployment, monitoring, and treatment.
Researchers provide guidelines for improving the treatment of hepatitis B.
In a recent study, researchers were able to explain how co-infection with Hepatitis B (HBV) and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV) can provide a treatment advantage over infection with HBV alone.
In Southern Africa, severe infection with HBV and HIV is a major problem.
Doctors need to understand how these pathogens and the drugs used to treat them interact, so that they can better diagnose and care for patients.
Researchers wanted to compare the effects of treatment on patients who have only HBV, with patients who have both HBV and HIV.
For this study, the researchers recruited 115 adult patients suffering from chronic hepatitis B (CHB).
They were recruited from Tygerberg Hospital in Cape Town, South Africa.
Some patients (39) were infected with HIV while the rest were infected with HBV only.
Researchers examined skin color, age, and gender, and conducted various clinical and laboratory tests.
Researchers found that patients with only HBV are unlikely to be on any form of antiviral treatment, showing symptoms of liver disease (since HBV is a virus that can cause severe liver disease).

Researchers were able to show that individuals who carry only HBV were in poorer health compared to those who carry both HIV and HBV, as patients infected with the virus would be on HIV treatment, which also provides an advantage in combating HBV.

Results from this study indicate the potential impact of differences between interventions and monitoring and treatment options for Hepatitis B compared to HIV and HBV, which prioritize those infected with HIV and HBV.
Researchers have shown that we must improve and provide safer and more equitable care for patients infected with HBV alone.
One limitation of this study is the small sample size which is restricted to only one country and their hospital system.
Some, perhaps more advanced hospital environments, may show differing opinions compared to what was found in this study.
Further research is needed to identify the exact differences found in this study.
This paper demonstrates the power of collaboration, with researchers working on this project from South Africa and the United Kingdom.
By using the large number of South African patients for this study, the research is relevant to a segment of the African population.
In addition, the study can help in providing improved treatment plans for those suffering from HBV, HIV, or both.
Assessing the Impact of Security Deterioration on Women's Business Activities in Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State.

This study analyzed the impact of insecurity on the business activities of women in Shiroro Local Government Area of Niger State, focusing particularly on issues related to women's financial independence, the types of business activities commonly engaged in by them, and the extent of the impact of insecurity on their business operations.
A sample of 377 women was studied, which led to the finding that women in Shiroro are highly entrepreneurial and financially independent, mostly engaging in SMEs.

The study also found that while insecurity adversely affects women's businesses through loss or reduction of capital among other factors, the number of women entrepreneurs did not experience a significant decline.

The study suggests that sustainable plans should be developed to improve women's access and use of financial services, as well as to establish and strengthen community policing groups to combat insecurity in the study area.
Female entrepreneurs in Niger need more security.
Researchers found that businesswomen in Niger were very entrepreneurial and financially independent, but security from criminals was a problem.

The researchers wanted to know how women conducting businesses in Shiroro Local Government Area in Niger State are in terms of safety and security, and how this could affect their businesses and their independence.
They discussed with 377 women in this field about the challenges they face in terms of business activities, financial independence, and insecurity.
They stated that 43% of women said they do not rely on men for financial support, and 32% said they have other people they depend on for financial support.
Researchers also found that 85% of women earn income from various occupations, and few reported relying on a salary.
About 56% earned income through farming, and 79% through business.
About 1 in 5 women earn money through hairdressing, sewing and knitting, or doing laundry.
The majority of women (91%) told researchers that the fear of being attacked by thieves and criminals affected their business.
They often lose money and even their husbands as a result of these attacks, sometimes even being forced to meet the demands of their children alone.
The women also stated that they do not have sufficient skills and funds to expand their businesses.
Researchers have stated that, despite these challenges, women in Niger have continued to make significant progress in their business endeavors.
They said Shiroro has people of different ethnicities and religions, and this is also good for business.
This study challenges the findings of other researchers who reported that women have less success in business due to their role as caregivers at home.
Instead, these researchers say that the success of female entrepreneurs in this region of Niger is more influenced by the threat of criminal attacks and thieves.
Researchers have suggested that all stakeholders should come together to combat factors that could hinder success in business.
For example, women in Niger should have increased access to finances, land, and security.
They also suggested that professional women could form groups that would help them combat thieves and criminals.
The Association of Blood Pressure with Selenium, Copper, and Zinc Levels During Pregnancy and the Risk of Preterm Birth: A Cohort Study from Malawi
Preterm birth is birth before the completion of 37 weeks.
A study was conducted to evaluate the relationship between blood levels of selenium, copper, and zinc and the birth of preterm infants.
There are 181 women in this particular study, 90/181 (49.7%) and 91/181 (50.3%) pregnant women before childbirth.

The mean concentration of selenium was 77.0; SD 19.4µg/L, copper was 2.50; SD 0.52 mg/L, and zinc was 0.77; SD 0.20 mg/L with reference ranges of 47-142µg/L, 0.76-1.59mg/L, and 0.59-1.11 mg/L, respectively.
The results indicate that there is no deficiency of selenium and zinc; and an excess of copper in pregnancy.
Preterm birth is associated with increased levels of copper and zinc.
The elements zinc and copper, as well as selenium compounds, are related to the birth of twins.

Researchers have discovered the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc minerals in women who have given birth to preterm babies, but they still do not know if these elements are derived from their diet.
Preterm birth occurs when a woman gives birth before completing 37 weeks of pregnancy.
Preterm birth is associated with adverse health outcomes for the infant, ranging from birth defects to death.
There are many causes of preterm birth, but the role of the abundance of nutritional minerals found in food and the environment is not known.
These nutrients are essential for the development of the baby, but researchers want to know what would happen if there are too many of them.

For this study, researchers aimed to measure the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc in women who have given birth to stillborns, and also to determine whether the occurrence of stillbirths is due to the excessive levels of each type of nutrient studied.
Researchers collected blood samples from 181 women immediately after childbirth at two hospitals in Lilongwe, the capital of Malawi, between June 2016 and March 2017.
They sent the blood samples to a laboratory in Norway where they extracted the blood cells, determined the best blood type, and measured the levels of selenium, copper, and zinc.
About half of the 181 women surveyed had given birth to twins, and researchers found high levels of selenium, copper, and zinc.

From there, they adjusted their calculations to account for various factors such as age, overall health, and pregnancy history to establish a basis for suspecting the effects that nutrients might have on the birth of twins.
They agreed that the levels of selenium and copper do not play a significant role in causing preterm birth, but the level of zinc increases the risk of preterm birth by more than six times.
The abundance of copper, however, remains a concern for researchers, due to its known toxic effects.

The participation of only 181 women in the study limited the researchers' ability to identify the risks associated with high levels of selenium, as the more appropriate number of participants would have been 600 women.
The daily diet of participants was not examined to identify potential sources of the three minerals, and the Body Mass Index (BMI) was not recorded.
This is the first study of its kind to measure the impact of selenium, copper, and zinc on pregnant women in Malawi.
Africa has the highest rates of preterm births - over 18% compared to Western countries at 5%, so researchers want to know if nutrition plays a role.
Home Range Characteristics and Habitat Preference of the Pancake Tortoise (Malacochersus tornieri) in Kenya
Animals exhibit unique spatial and temporal behaviors that enhance their survival.
Understanding such behaviors is an important step in effective conservation and management, especially for species that are facing threats.

In this study, we tested whether the wide-backed tortoise has the ability to return home if displaced and examined the site fidelity and range of the species in its natural habitats in Kitui County, Kenya.

A study was conducted on the behavior of 39 tortoises residing separately in 12 rock crevices from July 2020 to June 2022 through radio tracking and camera trapping combined with focal scan sampling and ad libitum sampling.

Fourteen of the tortoises were fitted with radio transmitters and relocated from their home burrows to other burrows that were distant from their home burrows, and their movements and behaviors were monitored.

Except for only two females that fit into the new burrows of the habitat, all other turtles attempted to make a home, with 46.15% of them following their path back to their original burrows accurately and 15.38% reaching areas believed to be within the boundaries of their home.
The success of the home undoubtedly provides strong evidence of the reliability of the location within the species.

A study on turtle nesting showed that there was no significant difference between the number of turtles initially found in nests with an average number over a sample period of 162 days (F(1,22) = 0.0699, P>0.05), further supporting the strong reliability of site fidelity in the species.
On the other hand, events from camera traps and ad libitum sampling also confirmed that the broad-shelled tortoises are territorial, with males defending their territories from other incoming males.
Wide-backed turtles that have disappeared possess an amazing ability of 'homing'.

Researchers made a surprising discovery while studying the behavior of the East African pancake tortoises (Malacochersus tornieri): the animals are able to find their way back home after being relocated to a distance.
Understanding how and why they do this can be crucial for the conservation of these rare crawling animals.
The behavior of seeking shelter exhibited by these turtles is called "homing," and many other animals are also capable of doing this.
Access to specific locations allows animals to return to food, mates, and shelter, which enhances their chances of survival and reproduction.

Although studies have been conducted on the nesting behavior of sea turtles and freshwater turtles, researchers in this study say we still know little about nesting in tortoises (terrestrial equivalent of turtles).
In this study, the researchers aimed to gain a better understanding of the behavior of wide-backed tortoises in their natural habitat within the rocky mountains of Kenya.
They studied the animals as they moved and fed, as well as when they rested in burrows or gaps in the rock.
Researchers observed groups of wide-backed turtles for nearly two years and set up cameras to record videos of the animals when they were not being watched.
They also attached radio signal transmitters to 14 turtles.
These are small devices that allow researchers to track the movement of animals and observe their behavior both day and night.
From there, the researchers relocated some of these tracked turtles to a new location, in order to study them more easily.
However, to the researchers' surprise, two of the turtles began returning to their original areas, between 1 to 2.5 kilometers from where they were relocated.
This was when the researchers decided to attempt to move many of the animals from their homes, to see if they would exhibit the same 'home' behavior.
Interestingly, about half of the turtles found their way back to the original burrows they lived in before being relocated, often traveling more than 1.5 kilometers to reach the location.
About 15% of them managed to move across the entire region, but they failed to locate the hole from which they were initially taken.
Researchers also found that different burrows generally have a number of turtles resting in them, which indicates that they consistently use the same resting places.
Camera images also show that male turtles are territorial, meaning they will fight with other males trying to enter their territory or burrow.

Researchers say this is the first time that nesting behavior has been observed in the wide-backed turtle, and their findings indicate that these animals prefer to stay and rest in one place whenever they can.
Their study did not reveal how turtles find their way home, therefore future research should focus on understanding this important issue.
In some cases, it is necessary to relocate animals to new areas for conservation, this information will help conservationists to protect turtles in their new habitat.
The research is a collaboration between scientists from Kenya and China, and it has enhanced our understanding of the homeostasis in turtles and other animals.
Plasma Drug Delivery at Its Site of Action in the Body of Excessive Oral and Intravenous Rifampicin in Patients with Cerebral Tuberculosis:
Randomized Controlled Trial
Higher doses of intravenous rifampicin may improve outcomes in bacterial meningitis but are not beneficial in severe cases.

We predicted that the plasma exposure of rifampicin would be similar between oral doses of 35 mg/kg of body weight and intravenous doses of 20 mg/kg, which are recommended for effective testing in meningitis.
We conducted a randomized group study on drug delivery in the body during a clinical trial to enhance antibiotic treatment for meningitis.
Participants with HIV and meningitis were recruited from hospitals in South Africa and were randomly assigned to one of the three rifampicin dosage groups:
standard (oral 10 mg/kg), overdose (oral 35 mg/kg), and intravenous (20 mg/kg).
A drug delivery sample was administered at its site of action in a robust body on day 3.
Data were presented using a sectional analysis, and the findings were compared using geometric mean ratios (GMRs).
Forty-six participants were sampled for drug delivery at the site of action in the body (e.g., bone, n = 17; excessive oral intake, n = 15; intravenous, n = 14).
The median CD4 count was 130 cells/mm3 (interquartile range [IQR], 66 to 253 cells/mm3).

The geometric mean area under the concentration-time curve from 0 to 24 h (AUC0-24) values for rifampicin were 42.9 mg·h/ml (95% confidence interval [CI], 24.5 to 75.0 mg·h/ml) for standard oral administration, 295.2 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 189.9 to 458.8 mg·h/ml) for higher than standard oral dose, and 206.5 mg·h/ml (95% CI, 154.6 to 275.8 mg·h/ml) for intravenous administration.

The Rifampicin AUC0-24 GMR is 1.44 (90% CI, 0.84 to 2.21) and the maximum concentration of the drug in the blood (Cmax) GMR is 0.89 (90% CI, 0.63 to 1.23) for oral administration compared to intravenous administration.
The rifampicin plasma AUC0-24 was higher after oral administration of 35 mg/kg than when used intravenously at a dose of 20 mg/kg in the initial days of tuberculosis (TB) treatment.
The results of the study support the use of oral rifampicin in the trial for meningitis.
High-dose medication can be tested on HIV patients suffering from TB meningitis.
Researchers have confirmed that it is beneficial to start testing whether the dosage of rifampicin can save HIV patients suffering from meningitis.
About 3 out of 5 people with HIV who also contract meningitis die from this disease that attacks the nervous system.
Survivors are often left with permanent damage to their nervous system and the major nerves that run from the brain.
This can affect their emotions and movements.
Some patients experience paralysis or weakness in parts of their body, or parts of their face or body become paralyzed.
Rifampicin, a potent antibiotic used against tuberculosis, is administered in capsule form to attempt to eliminate the bacteria that cause meningitis.
Severely ill patients often have difficulty swallowing pills.
Rifampicin can also be administered intravenously (into the veins) in liquid form.
Then, an injection is administered into the patient's vein to release the fluid within the body.
No test has yet been conducted to determine how the patient's body absorbs the medication when using this method.
Intravenous medication requires additional equipment, a hospital, and a skilled healthcare worker who knows how to properly administer an intravenous injection.
Therefore, it is not necessarily a choice in regions with limited resources in the world.
Doctors already know that rifampicin is not effective for the cerebrospinal fluid pathway, the meninges, and the skull, where bacteria can hide.
This is why it is necessary to administer more than the usual dose (amount) to effectively eliminate all pathogens in the patient's body.
However, researchers are not certain about how excessive consumption can be effective and safe.

Therefore, researchers from South Africa and the United Kingdom wanted to determine, using a small number of patients, whether it is appropriate to administer a higher dose of rifampicin either as a capsule or intravenously, and how their bodies would absorb each form.
It is important to know this before other researchers begin large trials, or experiments, where they plan to give patients a higher dose of rifampicin than usual.
One of the three forms of rifampicin medication was given to 46 South African HIV-positive individuals suffering from tuberculosis meningitis.
The first is the standard treatment for tuberculosis currently given to patients, a total of 10mg of rifampicin per kilogram of the patient's weight.
A group found an excessive amount of 35 milligrams per kilogram of the patient's body weight.
The third group received 20 milligrams per kilogram of body weight.
A blood sample was taken from the patients after three days.
From there, the researchers measured the amount of rifampicin in their blood (the plasma section of the blood).
Higher levels of rifampicin were found in patients who received multiple doses compared to those who received the drug intravenously or in a standard amount.
The average concentration of the drug in blood plasma is the same for both oral administration and intravenous administration.
These statistics are greater than when patients received only the standard amount.
According to the researchers, this indicates that the health of patients suffering from meningitis could improve if they receive a higher dose of rifampicin.
It does not matter whether they receive it as tablets or through injection – the important thing is that they are receiving an excessive amount, because their body can store a large quantity of it.
The results support the findings of tests conducted in Uganda and Indonesia.
Two small trials in Indonesia, for example, suggested that the lives of many patients could be saved if they were given a higher dose of rifampicin either orally or intravenously.
However, the unfortunate thing is that the researchers warned that fewer participants took part in this study than they initially hoped, which could affect their results.
The study was conducted in South Africa.
It supports the plan to conduct trials to test whether it is beneficial to give HIV patients suffering from cerebral tuberculosis a higher dose of rifampicin.
It is hoped that such a medication will save the lives of many people in Africa and other parts of the world where meningitis has become a major problem.
Can the combination of fertilizer and charcoal improve the quality of soil in extreme climates in the savanna region?
Soil degradation is a major obstacle to crop cultivation in the sub-Saharan region.
Numerous authors have reported the positive impact of charcoal and fertilizer on soil productivity.

In this study, a 30-day laboratory experiment was conducted using 120 g samples each of Haplic acrisol amended with corn straw biochar (cbio), rice husk biochar (rbio), coconut husk biochar (coco300 and coco700) or poultry manure (taki); and decomposed rice husk biochar (rcocomp) or corn straw biochar (cococomp) at an amendment level of 1% w/w: soil, respectively.

Some soil treatment experiments in the study included chicken manure and corn cob or rice husk charcoal (1% manure + 1% charcoal: 1% soil w/w), respectively, to investigate their effects on soil respiration, soil pH; soil microorganisms; exchange capacity; total carbon content, total nitrogen content, and available nitrogen compounds.
Charcoal and fertilizer used alone or together, with the charcoal fertilizer increased the soil pH by 0.28-2.29 pH compared to the unamended soil.
The soil respiration emitted from compost made with rice husks or corn husks, or a mixture of biochar and compost, is stronger than that which is not amended, which resembles that of biochar alone.
The TOC in untreated fertilizer and that combined with corn charcoal, which was treated, is higher than the untreated one by 37% and 117%, respectively.
The combination of rice husk charcoal and manure increased MBC by 132% while the addition of combined manure increased MBC by 247%, respectively, compared to the untreated control.
Finally, the study showed that both untreated and biochar-treated fertilizers improved soil parameters such as soil pH and MBC, and also enhanced soil C balance by improving TOC and reducing soil C.
Charcoal and manure improve soil for plants.
This study examined how charcoal, a porous substance with a high carbon content made from discarded biomass, can be used to improve soil conditions in the Sahara region of Africa.

Mutations can make the variants more transmissible (spreading quickly), and more resistant to vaccines and treatments.
This study contributes to ongoing efforts to catalog the global variations of SARS-CoV-2.
The result provides significant evidence that SARS-CoV-2 is rapidly evolving as it spreads to infect humans and evade immunity.
However, further research is needed to understand what the actual impact or functions of the spike protein mutations in the A.23.1 variant will be.
Researchers have recommended increased surveillance of genetic material to help us understand how variations in viruses respond to vaccines available in Uganda and other countries.
They also stated that monitoring international travel is important so that researchers can better understand how the virus spreads domestically.
What Makes a Woman?
A Specific Study for Preserving the Reasons and Circumstances of Female Circumcision in Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya
Female genital mutilation is a harmful practice that violates women's rights and has adverse health effects.
This paper presents the reasons and circumstances of female genital mutilation/cutting (FGM/C) in specific areas of three countries – Indonesia, Ethiopia, and Kenya.

Data was collected through household surveys with youth (ages 15-24) and through focus group discussions, in-depth interviews, and key informant interviews with youth and stakeholders in the year 2016 and also in the year 2017.
Descriptive statistics and thematic content analysis were conducted.
The results of the study confirmed some factors of FGM/C documented by previous research, noting that these factors are closely related to each other, and gender norms are the underlying cause.
In all three locations, these factors cause changes in women's bodies to produce a 'normal' body that is suitable for royal status.
This results in a 'clean body' in Indonesia, a 'tame body' in Ethiopia, and an 'adult body' in Kenya.
Healthcare workers and parents play a crucial role in decision-making regarding FGM/C in all areas.
In Kenya, specifically, young women are discussing the role they play in decision-making about FGM/C as they grow up during circumcision.

The study reveals how legal and social changes in each location have led to changes in the practice of FGM/C, resulting in the medicalization of FGM/C in Indonesia, reducing the age of cutting for girls in Kenya, and increasing the prevalence of FGM/C in Ethiopia.
Three occurrences showed a significant difference in the practice of FGM/C and the social meaning for young women and their communities.
There is a need to further investigate the role that parents play in decision-making.

Due to the relationship between different causes of FGM/C in each context, the study concluded that specific contextual strategies need to be implemented through interventions to create sustainable change.
To stop female genital mutilation, we first need to understand why it occurs.
Female genital mutilation, the practice of cutting or removing parts of the female body, still occurs illegally or secretly in countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.
Researchers say that understanding the reason why this happens is the key to stopping this harmful practice, as well as preventing the health and mental problems that women suffer as a result.
In parts of Africa and Asia, female genital mutilation (FGM), sometimes referred to as 'female circumcision', continues to be practiced.
Many people believe the falsehood that FGM is necessary for good hygiene or to keep women modest (without frivolous freedom and modesty), and also to ensure that they can bear children.
FGM is not required for any of these according to scientific evidence.
In many cases, however, children who have undergone FGM end up with health problems later in life, such as infectious diseases and difficulty urinating, as well as mental health issues.
Because this practice is harmful and violates women's rights, many countries have banned it, but people still do it secretly.
In this study, researchers aimed to gain a better understanding of why FGM occurs in different countries and what people believe about the practice.
Therefore, they collected data on FGM in the countries of Kenya, Ethiopia, and Indonesia.

In each country, researchers spoke with people about the practice, including parents, youth, traditional leaders, healthcare workers, and 'cutters' (elderly women who are accustomed to performing FGM on girls).
At times, they discussed with these individuals, but they also spoke with groups of people, including adults and youth, who have experienced FGM.
Researchers found that the reasons for FGM, how it is performed, and beliefs about the practice vary in each country.
They also found that many people are still doing it, even in places where it is prohibited.
For example, in Indonesia, traditional birth attendants use a knife or needle to cut a part of the clitoris (the organ responsible for sexual pleasure in women) when a girl reaches 40 days old.
People believe that this helps in 'removing impurities' and is important for religious reasons.
In Ethiopia, FGM occurs early, sometimes when infants are only 7 days old.
Researchers found that the people in the area believe that this will ensure that one day the girl will become a 'good woman', and she will be obedient, and will not be defiant towards her husband.
Many people also believe that FGM facilitates childbirth, but it can actually make childbirth more difficult instead.
In the current situation in Kenya, FGM indicates that a girl has become a woman, and it usually occurs later in life, when she is an adolescent.
In some cases, however, they found that girls could undergo FGM as early as age 8, and many girls become pregnant while still young, because they are considered ready for sexual activity after FGM.
Researchers stated that their study shows there are various reasons why FGM still occurs.
As laws and social norms change, the manner and location in which they are enacted also change.
For example, parents may attempt to do this secretly even though it is illegal, because they believe it is appropriate for their daughter to be in good health or to find a good husband.
It is important to recognize that because FGM is illegal in some areas, investigating the issue can be challenging, and people do not always provide truthful answers about the subject.

In the future, besides banning it, researchers say that governments and health authorities should aim to stop FGM by addressing the false beliefs people have about this practice and educating them about the risks.

This is a collaborative study between scientists from Ethiopia, Indonesia, and the Netherlands, and it is part of a larger initiative called the "Yes I Do programme," which aims to reduce teenage pregnancies, child marriages, and FGM.
Genetic Instability of Birth, Cell Death, Sperm Morphophenotypes, and Structural Changes in the Testes of Dinka Rats (Cricetomys gambianus, Waterhouse, 1840) Exposed to Sodium Metavanadate Mutation
Environmental exposure to vanadium has been increasing in recent days.
This metal is a known poison.
The current study was conducted to investigate the reproductive toxicity of sodium metavanadate (SMV) in Dinka rats.
SMV was administered daily for 14 consecutive days at a dose of 3 mg/kg of body weight.
Clean water was provided to the control group.
We studied the reproductive blood cells and sperm storage and quality, along with the ultrastructural changes of the testicular after SMV treatment.
Our results show that SMV expressed in the AGR group increased the growth of menstrual cycle-regulating cells statistically but decreased the concentration of testosterone, FSH, and LH.

Furthermore, the group subjected to SMV demonstrated a reduction in sperm motility and activity, along with an increase in abnormal spermatozoa morphophenotypes and the elevation of P53 apoptotic markers.
Ultrastructural analysis revealed vacuolation of germ and Sertoli cells in both the cytoplasm and nucleus; mitochondrial swelling and vacuolations were also observed.
There was severe disintegration of the seminiferous tubules, detachment of muscle, and destruction of myeloid cells, along with the death of Leydig and Sertoli cells and pathogens.

Ultimately, the appearance of intraperitoneal SMV causes adverse effects on certain reproductive blood cells, reduction in sperm reserve and quality, cell death, and degenerative changes in Leydig, Sertoli, and germ cells which can lead to infertility.
Researchers say that the metal found in polluted air causes rats to become infertile.
Researchers have discovered that vanadium, a type of metal, damages the cells of mice and their ability to reproduce (fertility).

Because this metal is also toxic to humans, they recommended further research to determine whether the metal increasingly found in our environment due to pollution could have the same harmful effects on human health.
Although vanadium is a metal, it can enter the air slightly when fuel and coal are burned.
As the world continues to use more of these petroleum methods, the amount of polluted vanadium compound is increasing.
We already know that people who have contracted the disease may suffer from health issues such as anemia, dry throat and eyes, and chest pain.
Recently, scientists have also become interested in the effects that the element vanadium might have on reproduction.
They began studying these effects in mice, which are commonly used in laboratories due to their similarity to humans.
In this study, researchers were interested in the effect of vanadium on a common type of rat found in West Africa, known as the Dinka Rat.
They wanted to understand how the element vanadium alters the reproductive system of male rats, particularly their sperm, genetic material, and their offspring's cells.
Researchers administered vanadium injections to 6 rats once a day for 14 days.
At the same time, they injected six other mice with water as a "control" experiment.
Because water rarely affects rats, researchers can confirm that any changes they observed in the first six rats are a result of the vanadium compound injection.
After 14 days, they checked whether the levels of genetic material, such as testosterone, had changed, and they examined their offspring and counted their sperm.
By using a technique called Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM), they were able to observe any changes that occurred within the tissues in detail, down to the level of individual cells.
Researchers found that rats injected with vanadium had lower levels of testosterone and other hormones that are important for reproduction.
Rats that were injected with vanadium also had low sperm count, and their sperm was unhealthy.
Researchers observed, for example, that some sperm from mice lacked heads or had bent tails, and did not move like sperm from mice injected with water.
Because their sperm are the male gametes, which are used to fertilize eggs in females, these changes will enable the mice to successfully reproduce.
Ultimately, the researchers found that some cells from the ovaries of the rats were severely damaged or even destroyed by the vanadium compound.
Researchers say the mutations they discovered could lead to complete infertility.
They observed that since animals exposed to vanadium and other environmental pollutants may be unable to reproduce, they might potentially become extinct due to these effects.
Because humans are mammals like rats, scientists should study any adverse effects of vanadium in a polluted environment on human health.

Researchers have warned that some of the changes found in animals and their cells differ from what previous scientific research has discovered, therefore, more work is needed to understand the effects caused by the vanadium compound.
This is a collaborative study between scientists from Nigeria and Egypt, and it addresses what scientists know about how environmental pollution affects animals and even humans.
The Cultural Uses of Indigenous Plants in the Indigenous Communities of Northwestern Ethiopia
The study of garden flowers in northwestern Ethiopia in general, particularly in the Gozamin district, has received little attention.
The aim of this study is to further understand the floral elements and cultural significance of home gardens.
A random sampling model was used based on agricultural diversity in selected regions.

Household plot data was collected by dividing the household plots into four sections: the first extending from the farmer's house to a distance of 10 meters, the second from 10 meters to 20 meters, the third from 20 meters to 30 meters, and the fourth from 30 meters to 40 meters horizontally, using the farmer's house as a reference point in relation to the size of the farm.
An interview was conducted to collect information from the informant about plant species.
A total of 238 important plant species from 81 families were identified.
Among these, 39% are herbs, 29% are shrubs, and 6% are climbers.
Perennial plants constituted the majority of the cultivated species (83%), while annuals made up the remainder (17%).
The Grass family has large numbers of species, with 22, which the Legume family contains, which has 21, and the Flower family which has 15.

Among these recorded plants, 140 (58.6%) were used for environmental purposes, 84 (35%) for food crop purposes, 83 (34.7%) as medicinal plant species, 39 (16.3%) as livestock species, 57 (23.8%) as utility plants, 60 (25%) as oil tree species, 50 (21%) as socially useful plants, and 1 (0.4%) as toxic.
The matrix status directly indicates that the Cordia Africana tree is an important cultural plant in the region, which is also the most threatened, followed by the Ficus sur tree.
The most valuable use of the Cordia africana tree is for construction, and its ranking value is medicinal.
The Sorensen similarity index for 64% of the sites surveyed was less than 0.5.
The results indicate that home gardens are highly functional, a long-term production system.
The knowledge of the cultures of tribes related to their home gardens supports food security and the conservation of biodiversity.
The lack of similarity/diversity in the area between kebeles indicates that there are significant variations, which is due to the different ranges of inactivity conditions among the kebeles.
Ethiopian gardens support food production and conservation.
Researchers say that many Ethiopians cultivate food crops, ornamental plants, medicinal plants, and plants for feeding animals, providing shade, or as hedges in their gardens.
They studied these gardens to see how important they are in ensuring food security and also in helping to preserve the environment.
Communities around the world maintain gardens for food, to earn money, and for other cultural reasons.
The gardens also protect important plants that are often absent or disappearing in other areas.
In Ethiopia, not much research has been conducted on what communities actually plant in their gardens.
In this study, the researchers aimed to investigate the plants cultivated by the people of the Gozamin district in northwestern Ethiopia in their gardens and what they use them for.
They identified and counted plants in 357 gardens in the area.
They also interviewed the community about the things they use the plant for.
Researchers found that all the farms in Gozamin are less than one hectare.
They collected and identified a total of 238 different plants.
Most (83%) of the plants are cultivated throughout the year, and only a few (17%) are seasonal.
Their results showed that communities used plants for food, medicine, construction, animal feed, and other cultural practices.
Many plants serve more than one purpose.
For example, the large-leaved tree of the North can be used for medicine, decoration, food, shade, fencing, and other cultural purposes.
More than half (59%) of the plants were used for environmental purposes such as hedges, shade, and decoration.
Researchers said it helped in protecting the environment.
Moreover, hedgerow plants have helped in protecting crops.
More than 35% of plants are harvested for food, such as fruits, vegetables, grains, and spices.
However, they said that the farms in the area produce more fruits.

Researchers stated that 35% of the plants are used as traditional medicine for the benefit of humans and animals, while 21% are used in religious and spiritual activities, smoking, perfumery, and hair care.
Some plants (17%) were used as food to feed cattle, sheep, and donkeys.
Some others (24%) were involved in construction tools and making gardening tools, roofing chains, and making ropes.
Since most rural residents are reported to use firewood, 25% of the plants were used for this purpose.
Researchers stated that only one plant (0.4%) was mentioned for toxic purposes.
Furthermore, they said that the distribution of plants in the area is influenced by the environment, what people prefer to eat, the financial status of families, and business demands.
For example, a region called Wenka, which has an irrigation channel and is near a major city, has many gardens and contains as many as 130 different plant species.
The people of Wenka also cultivate and produce fruits and vegetables for the town market.
Finally, the researchers stated that most farmers prefer to plant crops with multiple uses.
Researchers stated that their findings confirm that indeed farmers cultivate a variety of plant species in their gardens, with different uses.
Although these researchers found that most farmers grow vegetables, some researchers say that trees are more prevalent in the area.
The researchers of this study were from universities in Ethiopia.
